articles.title: Carlos Baleba is expected to make his Man Utd debut against Spurs
articles.summary: Manchester United's £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is expected to make his debut against Tottenham Hotspur at Old Trafford
articles.body:
Carlos Baleba has come a long way since the day he had to pull out of a Cameroon Cup last-16 match due to a school exam.

Now Baleba's exams tend to be restricted to the football field - and a significant one is looming at Old Trafford this weekend.

It is unfair on the 22-year-old to be viewed as the potential saviour of Manchester United's season.

However, at £70m, Baleba was by far the most expensive of United's three major summer signings.

He is also the player earmarked for the holding midfield role Michael Carrick has had trouble filling effectively following Casemiro's exit in May.

United knew Baleba had an ankle injury when they bought him from Brighton on 25 August and they may have to wait until after the international break for the Cameroon midfielder to make his debut.

They were not expecting that they would be 12th in the Premier League, with just one win and five points from their opening five games. In addition, Brighton came from 2-0 down at Old Trafford to deservedly knock them out of the EFL Cup.

So there is no disguising that the pressure is on for Baleba and his new club ahead of the visit of rock-bottom Tottenham before three away trips in a row. Champions League encounters at Atletico Madrid and Como fall either side of a journey across the Pennines to face Leeds.

"Very quick," is the assessment from one United insider of their first impressions of Baleba. "He covers the ground really well."

A handful of training sessions before Baleba was named on the bench for the 1-1 draw at Fulham on 20 September, and a closed doors game against Swiss League outfit Lausanne-Sports on 2 October, when United's international contingent were absent, is a small sample size to form an opinion on.

However, Baleba's speed is something that should bring positive benefits to United's midfield.

Andrey Santos has it; less so Kobbie Mainoo and Youri Tielemans, who have been paired together by Carrick in the last four league games due to their superior technical abilities.

United have been too easy to play through and danger has not been spotted quickly enough.

Carrick's side is one of only four in the top flight yet to keep a clean sheet. They have conceded twice in four out of their seven games in all competitions. Until an answer is found, an upturn in form is difficult to envisage.

Clearly, Baleba must do a bit more than run fast, and his input must be felt in the dressing room as well as on the pitch.

Sources say an understandable initial shyness and nervousness seems to be being overcome. Baleba is not the most confident English speaker, but he has improved significantly since he moved to Brighton from Lille for £23.2m in 2023.

He has struck up a friendship with Amad Diallo. It is coincidence two young players from Africa should be going through their recovery work at the same time, but also helpful that a shared background creates a natural bond that has been built on over the last few weeks.

Amad was even laughing on the video he uploaded onto social media of Baleba poking fun at him after Cameroon beat his Ivory Coast in a friendly on 3 October.

A former team-mate of new France international Leny Yoro at Lille and Bryan Mbeumo at international level, Baleba already has other unexpected relationships at United's Carrington training ground judging by his joking with Patrick Dorgu after the final game of last season at the Amex Stadium.

The key for United is that Baleba produces the performances that lit up his 2024-25 campaign and earned suggestions of a potential move to Real Madrid, rather than those last term which were often below-par.

Suggestions Baleba had his head turned by late interest from United in the summer of 2025 have been dismissed by Brighton sources, although an alternative reason for the dip in form has not been offered.

As it turned out, the background work done by the data and recruitment teams at Carrington 12 months ago was not wasted. After missing out on Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, and with other options deemed unsuitable, United moved for Baleba just before the shock opening-day defeat at Hull, completing the deal just afterwards.

Given they were being quoted significantly more than £100m for the midfielder in August 2025, they regard £70m as good business.

However, Baleba is yet to step on the pitch and as Fernandes has shown in his disappointing early performances for Tottenham, any early assessment of what constitutes a good deal should at least wait for that.

It will be fascinating to see how Baleba and Fernandes match up to each other if they start at Old Trafford, when defeat for either side has the potential to turn early season disappointment into a near crisis.

Baleba's natural jocular personality should help his preparation. He will hope to get the chance to show off his back flip goal celebration – even if an ability to find the net is not why United bought him.

More importantly though, he has a powerful determination to succeed, drilled into him by his dad. He pushed him through punishing training sessions when he was younger, which Baleba has said was integral to him becoming a professional.

In a sense, success has already been achieved given he has fulfilled a promise he made to his mum to build her a house in Douala. Tragically for Baleba, his mother died a few months before he left Lille and never saw it.

He is still pushing, still motivated to do well for her, as he recounted in an interview with the Guardian in April 2025.

Go back further, to a chat with French football magazine Onze Mondial in September 2023 and you get to the core of what makes Baleba tick.

In explaining his passions outside of football, Baleba talks about manga, described by the British Museum as 'Japanese comic books or graphic novels', which now has 'fans across the globe'.

His favourite series is Fist of the North Star, the hero of which is Kenshiro.

"When he started out, everyone beat him up, he got covered in scars, then he became strong," Baleba explained. "After that, he was the one beating everyone up. He never gave up. I like that attitude."

articles.title: David Soria, optimista con la llegada de Carvajal al Getafe: "Creo que se va a dar"
articles.standfirst: El guardameta azulón cree que el exjugador del Real Madrid llegará al Coliseum
articles.summary: El guardameta azulón cree que el exjugador del Real Madrid llegará al Coliseum
articles.body: Dani Carvajal todavía no es jugador del Getafe, pero en el vestuario azulón ya hay quien espera su llegada. David Soria se pronunció sobre la operación en El Larguero y dejó un mensaje rotundo sobre el futuro del exmadridista: "Creo que se va a dar". El guardameta considera que la incorporación del lateral sería un refuerzo de primer nivel para un equipo que afronta por delante unos meses especialmente exigentes, con LaLiga y Europa en el horizonte. Soria, además, habló desde la perspectiva de un compañero que ya imagina a Carvajal en el día a día de Bordalás. "Nosotros estaríamos encantados", aseguró. El capitán azulón entiende que el Getafe necesita efectivos para afrontar la acumulación de partidos y ve en el lateral una pieza especialmente valiosa por todo lo que puede aportar dentro y fuera del campo. "Un refuerzo como Carvajal, con toda la experiencia, el nivel y todo lo que conlleva un jugador así, sería un refuerzo de 10", explicó. El entusiasmo del vestuario contrasta, sin embargo, con una realidad que mantiene la operación bloqueada. Carvajal ya ha pasado el reconocimiento médico, pero el problema está en las condiciones económicas de su incorporación. LaLiga ha activado su Órgano de Validación para determinar si el salario planteado por el Getafe se ajusta a los parámetros de mercado y al control económico. Un procedimiento que se ha convertido en el principal obstáculo para que el fichaje se haga realidad. Por tanto, ahora el Getafe debe encontrar la fórmula que permita encajar la operación dentro de su límite salarial y de los criterios establecidos por LaLiga Soria, pese a conocer las dificultades, mantiene el optimismo. Incluso se permitió bromear con la situación y con la capacidad de maniobra del presidente azulón: "Vamos a ver si el presidente se inventa algo y podemos llegar a un acuerdo". Una frase que refleja la confianza que existe dentro del vestuario en que las negociaciones terminen llegando a buen puerto. Soria, al menos, lo tiene claro: "Creo que se va a dar".

articles.title: Simone Magill: 'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'
articles.summary: Northern Ireland striker Simone Magill tells BBC Sport NI about balancing motherhood with her return to football and how her life has changed since giving birth to daughter Skye earlier this year.
articles.body:
"Football will always be a large part of my life but it's very much what I do, not who I am.

"Ultimately, I'm Skye's mum and, to me, that's the most important thing."

Through her 16-year footballing career, Simone Magill has been something of a trailblazer in Northern Ireland.

From a senior debut at the age of 15, helping the country to a major tournament debut and becoming captain, she has been there and seen it all.

But after giving birth to her first child, Skye, in May, her focus is paving the way off the pitch, as well as on it.

"I think we get labelled as athletes, and that is our complete entire identity," Birmingham City striker Magill told BBC Sport.

"Obviously there's been a massive shift now. I'm a mum first and foremost and that is the highest title that I will ever have.

"Family is so important. It's my priority, and it's so nice for me to have that greater purpose now.

"It's hard and it can be overwhelming, but it's the greatest joy that I've ever experienced in my life."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil

Magill is speaking at the Northern Ireland camp in the lead up to Friday's World Cup play-off with Portugal.

While she is stepping up her training four months on from giving birth, the first round of play-offs have come too soon.

However, after conversations with manager Michael McArdle, who has spoken about the importance of family , the 31-year-old is in camp to train with the squad.

More importantly, Skye and her husband, Mark, are with her for the duration.

It is a glimpse into what the future will look like when Magill is back playing for Northern Ireland.

"It's so different, but it's so special. I'm really enjoying being back in, and I think I find it weirder having my husband here than having Skye," she said.

"It's just amazing that I'm able to do this and the support that I've been given to allow me to do this has made things so much easier."

After nearly a year away from the squad, from when she announced her pregnancy last November, she says the support that the Irish FA and her Northern Ireland team-mates have provided has meant "I don't need to worry about anything".

Skye and Mark have become fully integrated in the camp and join the team for meals and in downtime.

Then, when it comes to on-pitch matters and meetings, Mark is able to look after Skye and Magill can focus on the football side of things.

"Mark has his daddy-daughter days with her while I'm on the training pitch.

"Then when I'm here with the girls in and around the hotel and free times, we're all here mingling with Skye.

"She's now got 23 aunties who are all very hands-on."

Before camp, Magill admits there was a bit of apprehension about how integrating back into the group with Skye may look, but "I feel a sense of obligation to pave the way".

While she is not the first Northern Ireland player to have a child and return to playing - experienced defender Sarah McFadden gave birth to her second child in 2024 - Magill is the first to have the family integrated into the camp.

"So it's the unknown of what things are going to look like," she said.

"It's relatively new in the game and I suppose I'm one of the first people certainly here and at club as well to do this.

"There are going to be certain things that we might need a little bit more support with, but we don't know that until we go through each phase and we're navigating that all collaboratively."

'Can I still play if I can't bring her?'

Magill feels that having Skye with the group is "lovely for the mood" and "gets everyone involved" as the new arrival is the most popular member of the camp.

She added that having Skye and Mark in camp has been "game-changing", and pointed to how a new mother in a more traditional job would have a year off, while her career means she is looking to get back on the pitch as quick as possible.

"If I didn't have that support then it almost questions, 'can I still play football if I can't bring her?'

"But it means that I can fully focus on being a footballer, but equally put everything into still being a mum at the same time."

While Skye has yet to be given a club team to support - Magill has played for Everton and Aston Villa before joining Birmingham and Mark supports Manchester United - there is no debate surrounding her international allegiance.

Despite Mark being from England, Skye has already been decked out in a mini-Northern Ireland kit.

"It's so important for me that she can come back to Northern Ireland often and just be surrounded by Northern Irish accents, to show her where I've come from and my roots. It's really special."

Magill said that she and Mark, who got married in 2021 after meeting at university, had always wanted to start a family and "we almost had to remove football from that decision".

While she stopped playing matches when she found out she was expecting, she was still active in training and the gym right up to a few weeks before Skye was born.

Just four weeks after her arrival, Magill was back doing gym work and she was back on the pitch after 13 weeks.

Now fully training again, she hopes to be back playing matches later in the autumn.

"It's funny because when I announced my pregnancy, I think the natural assumption from a lot of people in the scope of wider things thought that that was probably going to be the end of my football career.

"But I was like, 'well, no, absolutely not'.

"I very much wanted to be a voice and showcase that you can be a mum and a footballer, and those things can both co-exist."

Magill has spent longer away from playing matches than when she sustained an ACL injury at Euro 2022, but the stresses of rehab are absent.

For Magill, Skye has given her a new drive and purpose. Only five games away from a century of international caps, she dreams of walking out onto the pitch with her in her arms.

"Skye will not necessarily remember any of this, but I will.

"When she's older she can look back and see the hard work that I put in to come back and play, and it was all for her.

"All throughout my pregnancy I was almost manifesting that moment that when I make my return and being able to carry her out onto the pitch, I think, you know, that's what's driving me."

Magill said that McFadden was a role model for her when it came to balancing family and football, and now she wants to inspire other players to take the same step.

"We have a lot of younger members in the squad now and hopefully it is a very normal thing for them to see that this can be done.

"You know that there's a player playing for the team that has a child and she's able to bring the child in.

"That's very important to be normalised now in our sport and I'm just so thankful that the support systems are in place to allow me to do this.

"I've always wanted to inspire people on the pitch, but hopefully this is something I've done off the pitch that could also inspire future generations to show that it's possible."

articles.title: More than just football: How scandal-tainted City led Manchester's rebirth
articles.summary: Standing behind the counter of his fish-and-chip shop near the Etihad Stadium, Sailish Parekh says the transformation of east Manchester over the past two de...
articles.body:
Standing behind the counter of his fish-and-chip shop near the Etihad Stadium, Sailish Parekh says the transformation of east Manchester over the past two decades has been remarkable.

Manchester City "has not only just been a football club for the area. It's a bit of a saviour, to be honest," he told AFP.

Before City -- now embroiled in the biggest financial scandal to hit football's cash-rich Premier League -- moved to the area it was "very deprived" with high rates of unemployment, he said.

Since the club's takeover by deep-pocketed Abu Dhabi investors in 2008, long-neglected districts between the stadium and the city centre have become symbols of the northern city's rebirth.

Decades of decline linked to deindustrialisation have been reversed.

In neighbourhoods such as Ancoats and New Islington, red-brick warehouses still stand as reminders of Manchester's industrial past.

But many disused mills and factories have given way to apartment blocks, trendy cafes and co-working spaces.

Software engineer Simon Martin, 44, who lives in Ancoats, recounted how a cab driver told him he would have hesitated once to pick him up, when the area was riddled with crime.

Today, Martin praises the "really nice community" with "more young families moving in", although soaring rents have pushed out some lower-income residents.

The transformation reflects the influence of Manchester City and its owner, Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG), controlled by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family.

The Emirati investors have not just turned City into one of Europe's dominant football clubs.

They have also poured money into property development, building homes and commercial spaces on council-owned land leased under favourable terms.

The partnership is centred on Manchester Life, a property company created jointly between ADUG and the council in 2014, but it has drawn criticism over transparency and profit distribution.

In a 2024 study, University of Sheffield researchers argued the arrangement primarily enabled the ADUG group to lock in rising land values.

The city council rejects the criticism, saying it secured "the best overall deal" at a time when investors were scarce after the 2007-2008 global financial crisis.

According to the council, the partnership delivered around 1,500 homes and nearly 2,800 square metres (30,100 square feet) of commercial space.

The debate has resurfaced after the Premier League announced last week that an independent commission had found the club guilty on more than 100 charges of breaking financial rules.

It has been accused of artificially inflating revenues and reduced reported costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.

No sanction has yet been announced but City could face substantial points deductions, a fine or even expulsion from the Premier League. It could also face compensation claims from other clubs.

With both Manchester City and rivals Manchester United having huge international draw, football is one of the city's defining assets, said Subrahmaniam Krishnan-Harihara, head of research at the Greater Manchester Chamber of Commerce.

"This is our Eiffel Tower. I think without football, the brand value would not be this big," he told AFP.

According to consultants EY, Premier League-related activity generates around £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion) in annual revenues across Greater Manchester.

The city also attracts about 1.7 million overseas visitors each year.

Manchester City was a "catalyst" for infrastructure projects, including the expansion of the tram network, said Krishnan-Harihara.

Club officials say more than £700 million has been invested since 2008 in the Etihad Campus and surrounding districts, where sports facilities, a sixth-form college, a velodrome, retail developments and the Co-op Arena concert venue have emerged.

The Abu Dhabi investors were "key", said Georgina Blakeley, a professor at the University of Huddersfield who highlighted the impact of the 2007-2008 crash.

"You really get that turning off of the tap of regeneration activity ... and austerity hit cities like Manchester particularly hard," she said.

The Manchester Life project became part of the so-called "Manchester model", an urban development strategy championed by the council in the early 2000s and backed by Andy Burnham, the Greater Manchester mayor from 2017 to 2026 who is now UK prime minister.

Burnham sparked controversy recently when he said he would be "really concerned" should the Emirati owners walk away over the finance charges.

His office later sought to clarify the remarks, insisting "there can't be any suggestion that anyone is above the rules".

But Krishnan-Harihara believes any sanctions imposed on the club are unlikely to inflict lasting damage on Manchester's economic prospects.

"The foreign direct investment pool is actually widespread because there are other countries, other sectors which are also attracting investment," he said.

Fish-and-chip shop owner Parekh agreed. Manchester is now "quite a lot" more than "the two football clubs," he argued.

articles.title: ¿'Invasión banana' en Anfield? La vieja tradición reaparece en plena crisis del Manchester City
articles.standfirst: El histórico símbolo de la afición 'cityzen', nacido en los años 80 y ligado incluso a la lucha contra el racismo, puede convertirse este fin de semana en una respuesta visual y pacífica al terremoto provocado por el caso financiero del Manchester City
articles.summary: El histórico símbolo de la afición 'cityzen', nacido en los años 80 y ligado incluso a la lucha contra el racismo, puede convertirse este fin de semana en una respuesta visual y pacífica al terremoto provocado por el caso financiero del Manchester City
articles.body: Anfield se prepara para recibir este fin de semana a un Manchester City que llega envuelto en uno de los momentos más delicados de su historia reciente. Tras el veredicto sobre los cargos financieros de la Premier League y la posterior apelación presentada por el club, el ambiente promete ser especialmente hostil para los de Enzo Maresca. En las comunidades de aficionados cityzens se respira un sentimiento de unidad y resistencia, y eso ha llevado a muchos a preguntarse si volverá a aparecer uno de los símbolos más peculiares de la cultura del club: las bananas inflables. Sin embargo, para entender qué significaría una eventual "invasión amarilla" en Anfield hay que viajar casi 40 años atrás. La explicación más documentada sobre el origen de esta costumbre procede tanto de la propia web oficial del Manchester City como del trabajo del historiador del club, Gary James. Todo comenzó el 15 de agosto de 1987, en un partido entre el City y el Plymouth Argyle. Un aficionado llamado Frank Newton acudió al encuentro con una enorme banana hinchable que provocó risas y se convirtió en centro de atención entre los seguidores. Lo que parecía una simple ocurrencia acabó transformándose en uno de los fenómenos más icónicos de las gradas inglesas. Newton siguió llevando la banana a otros desplazamientos y pronto comenzaron a aparecer más hinchables. La moda creció de forma espontánea hasta convertirse en una seña de identidad del City de finales de los años ochenta, cuando militaba en la segunda categoría del fútbol inglés. Con el paso de los meses, las gradas dejaron de estar ocupadas únicamente por bananas. Dinosaurios, tiburones, monstruos, martillos gigantes y todo tipo de figuras inflables acompañaban a la afición cityzen en cada desplazamiento. La propia versión oficial del club recuerda aquella época como una reacción de humor en medio de uno de los periodos más grises del fútbol inglés, marcado por el hooliganismo, las restricciones a los clubes ingleses tras la tragedia de Heysel y la pérdida de atractivo de las gradas. Según Gary James, el fenómeno alcanzó dimensiones extraordinarias durante la temporada 1988-89 y especialmente en el Boxing Day de 1988, cuando miles de aficionados del City acudieron al campo del Stoke cargados de disfraces e hinchables. El fenómeno fue tal que incluso al delantero Imre Varadi se llegó a apodar en tono jocoso Imre Banana en Maine Road. La historia adquiere una dimensión mucho más profunda cuando aparecen el estadio de Anfield y el Liverpool vinculados a las bananas. Concretamente por un futbolista de esta época: John Barnes. Diversas publicaciones recientes explican que las bananas acabaron adquiriendo con el tiempo un significado asociado a la lucha contra el racismo en el fútbol inglés. Durante los años 80, lanzar bananas a futbolistas negros era una práctica habitual en numerosos estadios británicos y una de las víctimas más conocidas de aquellos abusos fue Barnes, estrella del Liverpool y de la selección inglesa. La famosa imagen de Barnes apartando una banana con el pie durante un partido se convirtió en una de las fotografías más simbólicas de aquella época. Algunas publicaciones sostienen que los aficionados del City contribuyeron posteriormente a resignificar ese símbolo, transformando un objeto asociado al odio racial en una expresión festiva y comunitaria. No obstante, es importante precisar que las fuentes históricas más cercanas al origen, sitúan el nacimiento de la tradición principalmente en el humor y la cultura popular de las gradas, no en una campaña organizada contra el racismo. El estadio del Liverpool está inevitablemente ligado a la memoria de uno de los futbolistas que más sufrió el racismo en el fútbol inglés. Por ello, el posible regreso masivo de las bananas a Anfield encierra una paradoja histórica: De sucederse la citada invasión, un símbolo que durante décadas estuvo vinculado a algunos de los episodios más oscuros de las gradas inglesas volvería al escenario asociado a una de sus víctimas más emblemáticas, pero esta vez de la mano de una afición que lo considera parte de su propia identidad cultural. Sin embargo, hay quien podría plantearse si esta supuesta llamada a la movilización está relacionada con la crisis institucional que vive en estos momentos el Manchester City tras ser declarado culpable de los cargos que se les imputaba, A priori, y tratándose de una tradición que se remonta tanto en el tiempo, no parece que tenga mucho que ver, sobre todo, por dicha tradición nació en 1987. Lo que sí muestran los foros de aficionados, como puede ser Bluemoon, es un clima de cierre de filas alrededor del club a las puertas de la visita a Anfield. No en vano, en las últimas semanas del parón de selecciones prácticamente no se ha hablado de otra cosa en Inglaterra, valorando cuál debería ser la pena para los cityzens. En ese contexto, una presencia visible de bananas en la grada visitante podría interpretarse como un gesto de orgullo, desafío y pertenencia. No tanto una protesta organizada contra la Premier League como una declaración visual de apoyo a un club que siente que atraviesa un momento más que complicado de su historia reciente. De un modo u otro, y como confirmó el propio Erling Haaland hace unos días, pase lo que pase "los aficionados del City que vayan a Anfield se lo van a pasar bien". "Tenemos que mantenernos unidos, estar unos con otros, mantenernos positivos. Pase lo que pase en la vida, siempre tenemos que sonreír, mantenernos positivos, mirar hacia adelante e intentar ganar partidos de fútbol, disfrutar de la situación", reconoció el noruego.

Real Madrid midfielder Fede Valverde is questionable to face Villarreal this Saturday, coach José Mourinho announced during today's pre-match press conference. Mourinho did not disclose Valverde's issue, but it looks like the Uruguayan midfielder could sit this one out as Real Madrid get ready for a crucial stretch of the 2026-27 season.

In other news, Eder Militao will also miss the upcoming games even though he's already rejoined the squad in training. The Brazilian defender needs to keep improving his conditioning in order to make sure he stays healthy and fresh when he officially comes back from his injury.

articles.title: Nationally-ranked IMG Academy brings star-studded roster to New Palestine
articles.summary: IMG Academy is ranked No. 4 in the country. The Florida-based program brings star-studded roster to New Palestine.
articles.body:
What is New Palestine's football program up against when IMG Academy visits Hancock County on Friday night?

Stars. Enough to light up the night sky.

Florida-based IMG Academy is ranked No. 4 in the country by USA TODAY and No. 6 by High School Football America. The Ascenders have 19 four-star players on the roster, including edge rusher Jackson Vaughn, a Notre Dame recruit with 15 tackles for loss and five sacks, and the top-rated junior quarterback recruit in the country in Georgia commit Jayden Wade.

Indiana high school football's best 25 teams after Week 6

This game only came about because of the defections of New Castle and Shelbyville from the Hoosier Heritage Conference. New Palestine added Roncalli, which it lost to 20-6 last week, and IMG Academy to fill out the nonconference schedule.

The IMG game came about after former New Palestine assistant and current Cascade coach Nick Brickens joked with coach Kyle Ralph in the spring that they should fill one of the open spots on the schedule with IMG. Two days later, Ralph got a text from IMG's director of football operations that the program was looking for an opponent.

At first, he thought he was being pranked. But then he thought: Why not?

"My policy since I got here, when Al Cooper hired me, is that we would not be afraid to play anybody," said Ralph, who is 160-16 in 14 years at New Palestine with five state championships. "No matter the state of our program, if someone asks to play, we're going to try to rise to that occasion and play. If we have an opening and somebody calls, we're going to play them. … I want our program built off competition and I want our kids to find out what they are made of. You can't do that if you shy away. You take adversity head-on and come through it a little more polished than what you were."

New Palestine does have ranked recruits. Senior tight end and Kansas commit Mason Oglesby is a four-star prospect on the 247Sports composite. Junior defensive lineman Sam Hirschy is a four-star prospect in the 2028 class. Kaeden Ralph, a junior lineman, has an offer from UConn. So does junior safety Andrew Davis.

IMG has visited Indiana previously, defeating the 2023 Ben Davis team 34-14. It was the only loss for the Giants in a Class 6A state title season. Wade, the Georgia recruit, has completed 69.5% of his passes for 1,188 yards and 16 TDs with no interceptions and rushed for 182 yards and three TDs.

But he is far from a one-man band. Osani Gayles, a four-star receiver headed to Alabama, has 25 catches for 552 yards and seven TDs. Eric McFarland, a four-star receiver headed to Texas A&M, has 20 receptions for 425 yards and seven TDs. Cornerbacks Aaryn Washington and Censere Gaylord are committed to USC and Washington, respectively. Junior running back Elijah Newman-Hall is committed to Ohio State.

The list goes on and on. If you don't catch them Friday, IMG Academy will be on ESPN2 next week against NFL Academy out of London.

articles.title: Everton have been put up for sale
articles.summary: The breaking news on Friday morning is that Everton are up for sale. The turbulence continues on the blue half of Merseyside.
articles.body:
The breaking news on Friday morning is that Everton are up for sale.

The turbulence continues on the blue half of Merseyside.

Everton put up for sale only 22 months after they were taken over.

The car crash club once again looking for new owners.

Everton fans were left dismayed at a summer transfer window that saw the club make a net profit.

Quite clearly these owners not having the answers to turn around the crisis club that they took over in December 2024.

The official statement from the Everton owners declaring: 'The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest. When TFG became custodians of Everton, the Club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the Club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters. With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton. We will only entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the Club forward and build on the momentum that has been established…Moelis & Company has been retained by TFG.'

You would have to be naive in the extreme to believe that the owners of any major Premier League club are acting in anything but their own interests, whether that be Everton, Newcastle United, Liverpool and so on.

These Everton owners clearly have found out very quickly that they have a club that is in such a desperate state that they need to get out of it ASAP.

Interesting to see who might buy it, probably yet another American owner, which is now the case across most of the Premier League.

articles.title: Mourinho: "Si pitan a Mbappé será una victoria para vosotros"
articles.standfirst: El técnico portugués comparece ante los medios antes del regreso del Real Madrid a la competición tras el parón internacional
articles.summary: El técnico portugués comparece ante los medios antes del regreso del Real Madrid a la competición tras el parón internacional
articles.body: Mourinho cierra filas con sus jugadores. Con Mbappé en el centro de las críticas y el Bernabéu convertido en el termómetro de la paciencia del madridismo, el portugués lanza un mensaje de protección a su vestuario: no está dispuesto a señalar a sus futbolistas ni a dejar que el ruido exterior haga mella en el grupo. Parón de selecciones: "Es rival complicado, de Champions. Juegan muy bien y que todavía no tienen los puntos que van a tener. Tras perder el último partido tenemos la necesidad de sacar los 3 puntos. No ha sido fácil. Nos quedamos aquí con 5 jugadores y los otros fueron llegando después de su último partido con sus selecciones y tras los pocos días libres que hemos podido dar" Mbappé: "Si pasa eso para vosotros, no lo digo en nadie en particular, será una victoria. De hecho en las últimas semanas yo pensaba que tenía casos suficientes reales en el mundo del fútbol... pero parece que no ha sido suficiente. Ni casos gigantes como el City, la difícil situación de mi país de Cristiano con su entrenador. Tantos casos que podrían alimentar vuestro trabajo, pero no ha sido suficiente. El Madrid es el Madrid y siempre hay que sacar algo" ¿Es todo exagerado?: "Ridículo" Más sobre Mbappé y su recuperación (bici, vacaciones...): "Para mí un jugadores es 24 horas por día y lo vuelvo a decir. Si hacen algo a nivel privado, tiene siempre una repercusión. Un jugador de fútbol será siempre un ser humano, que se puede equivocar aquí y allá... pero siempre tendrá el sentido de la responsabilidad. Yo no miento, a todos los niveles. En este periodo los jugadores del Madrid han sido ejemplares en su situación profesional. Hemos trabajado aquí para que estuvieran bien. Todo perfectamente definido y controlando el descanso. Todos los que han viajado ha cumplido... y los lesionados han venido a Valdebebas, han tenido sus diagnósticos y han seguido su recuperación. Por ejemplo, Arda... que se lesionó en el último partido, he sido yo quien le ha dado dos días libres. El ejemplo vuestro de Mbappé, ha estado aquí, se hizo el diagnóstico y se fue para una segunda opinión porque tiene algo en la rodilla que no se puede olvidar. Durante la recuperación, que vosotros no tenéis que saber al detalle, y luego entramos en el campo de la búsqueda por problemas. Primero era la discoteca que no era discoteca... era una discoteca por la moda en París para un evento privado. Después la bicicleta en Suiza, que era un hotel en el que había un par de bicicletas para ir al spa, a las zonas comunes y de tranquilidad absoluta. Y llegamos a casos menores, el pobre de Huijsen, que estaba parado en la casa de Pitarch y estaba mandando un mensaje y parecía casi un criminal. Es ridículo. Queréis una historia... yo os la doy. Es la primera vez que el Madrid en octubre no tiene lesionados, los que hay son de la temporada pasada. Es una buena historia, pero no os gusta" Diomande: "No te respondo objetivamente... y no quiero decir cual es el equipo que va a jugar. El Madrid puede jugar con cualquiera de los jugadores de la plantilla porque tenemos mucha gente con calidad" ¿Entendería que parte de la afición estuviera molesta con Mbappé?: "Esto es uno de vuestros objetivos. No es necesario ser Einstein para entender que este es el objetivo. De quien prefiero no hablar, me puedo equivocar, pero es uno de los objetivos. Del Bernabéu. no comento. Respeto. Mi esperanza es que el Bernabéu sea capaz de ser justo. Ser justo es ser inteligente. Leer entre líneas y entender dinámicas. Entender los objetivos. Yo prometo que un jugador del Madrid no se comporte como jugador del Real Madrid y falle como jugador del Real Madrid, no cumple con sus obligaciones como jugador o como ciudadano, no van a ver ese jugador en banquillo. No van a poder pitarlo. Va a estar en casa. No le doy la oportunidad de sentarse en el banquillo. Mbappé va a jugar. Ni en el banquillo estará. Estoy seguro de que no ha fallado con sus obligaciones con el Real Madrid" Konaté, Militao y Valverde: "Fede es la duda, Militao no es duda porque no va a estar... pero verlo entrenar y cómo lo está haciendo me alegra. Yo bromeo cada día con él y los fisios: 'Vas a jugar'. Yo sabía que era bueno, pero es aún mejor. No va a estar ni mañana, ni Roma... necesita un par de semanas. Mendy entra por primera vez en campo con nosotros y Rodrygo está lejos aún. Hoy decidiremos cómo va a ser mañana" Meritocracia: "Meritocracia, si, pero también una abertura no para el nombre, pero sí para el momento. Saber lo que puede ser la mejor manera de ayudar a un determinado jugador. Hay jugadores que cuando no están bien hay estrategias para que mejore. Una es la meritocriacia pura y si no estás bien, estás fuera. Tiene riesgos. Hay jugadores que toman tiempo para volver a su nivel normal. Tú te refieres a Vini. Yo no me escondo. La cosa que me hace mal, que me deja triste, es entender que él quiere estar bien, quiere ser el que gana partidos, que hace la diferencia. Lo que me hace mal es sentir este dolor que él siente siendo un chico que para mi sorpresa es extraordinario y trabaja mucho para volver. ¿Va a jugar siempre hasta que vuelva o llegará un momento que haya un plan específico que no juega o que vaya a banquillo y encontrar otro modo? Yo, al madridismo verdadero, no toco. Solo respeto. Pero me hace mal al corazón, cuando un chico como esté que no está en este Vini que es de otro mundo, me hace mal que la gente influenciada por muchos de vosotros no le está ayudando. Merece ser ayudado. Quiere mucho ser el Vini que ha dado tantas alegrías al madridismo"

articles.title: Former Barcelona forward reveals brutal reality of Hansi Flick’s training sessions: ‘I used to leave feeling dizzy’
articles.summary: Hansi Flick’s demanding approach to training has become a defining feature of his time at Barcelona.He is known to demand maximum intensity from his players,...
articles.body:
Hansi Flick's demanding approach to training has become a defining feature of his time at Barcelona.

He is known to demand maximum intensity from his players, irrespective of whether it is training, a friendly or a Champions League match.

Rodri, who joined Barça from Manchester City in the summer, spoke about being overwhelmed by the intensity after his first few training sessions.

Former Blaugrana forward Pau Victor has now offered a revealing insight into just how physically exhausting those sessions can be.

Pau Victor reveals Flick's intense methods

Speaking to Que T'hi Jugues , Victor explained that Flick's reputation as an intense and demanding coach is entirely justified.

"Flick is very intense. I used to leave his training sessions feeling dizzy," Victor admitted.

"There are videos where you can see me and Gavi lying on the ground with our legs in the air."

"All the fame he has for being tough and demanding is completely true."

The former Barcelona forward's comments provide an interesting glimpse into the physical standards Flick expects from his players.

Pau Victor could not find a place under Flick. (Photo by Alex Caparros/Getty Images)

His recollection of training alongside Gavi also highlights the level of effort demanded even from footballers already accustomed to playing at the highest level.

Why Flick demands so much from Barcelona

The German coach's football relies heavily on intensity, particularly when Barcelona lose possession.

His aggressive pressing system requires players to react immediately, close down opponents and maintain their positioning even when physically exhausted.

That approach explains why Flick places such importance on fitness during training. Barcelona cannot consistently defend high up the pitch unless their players are capable of repeating demanding runs throughout matches.

The intensity Victor describes is therefore closely connected to the team's tactical identity rather than simply being a question of physical conditioning.

Flick's biggest challenge is keeping that intensity sustainable

The more interesting question is how Barcelona can maintain these standards across an entire season without overloading their players.

Raphinha is the perfect archetype Hansi Flick forward. (Photo by Judit Cartiel/Getty Images)

With La Liga , the Champions League and international commitments placing significant demands on the squad, recovery and rotation will become increasingly important.

This is particularly relevant for players such as Gavi, whose aggressive playing style involves constant movement, pressing and physical challenges.

Flick's Barça tend to constantly outrun teams in Europe, and they do not need to look beyond their captain Raphinha for an example.

The Brazilian is the one who sets an example for the rest of the team to follow , and they seem to be at their best yet this season.

It remains to be seen whether Flick's methods can get Barça closer to the elusive Champions League trophy, hopefully in the ongoing season.

articles.title: How do Spanish football clubs become 'Real' and what does it mean?
articles.summary: The title of 'Real' is bestowed upon Spanish clubs by the country's monarchy but it has little to do with achievements on the field.
articles.body:
You will have heard the names of Spanish clubs like Real Madrid, Real Sociedad and Real Betis.

But what does the word 'Real' actually mean?

It's translated simply to 'Royal' and it is not just a decorative addition to a club's name, or a title awarded to clubs for winning trophies.

It is a historic distinction connected to Spain's monarchy and one that has been carried by some football clubs for more than a century.

The top two Spanish divisions currently feature 11 clubs who carry the royal designation in their names.

In La Liga, they are Real Madrid, Real Betis, Real Sociedad, Real Racing Club, Real Club Celta de Vigo, Real Club Deportivo Espanyol and Real Club Deportivo de A Coruna.

In the second tier, they are Real Club Deportivo Mallorca, Real Oviedo, Real Sporting de Gijon and Real Valladolid.

So how does a club become 'Real' or 'Royal'?

The story goes back to the reign of King Alfonso XIII, who took an interest in the rapidly developing sport of football.

The first Spanish football organisation to receive the distinction was Real Club Deportivo de A Coruna.

The club's own history says Alfonso XIII granted it the title of 'Real' in 1909, while he also accepted the honorary presidency, which was the most direct way to earn the royal title.

A crown was added to the club's badge providing a visible symbol of its new royal patronage.

Real Sociedad, based in San Sebastian, was the next to get the seal of approval, in 1910. The distinction carried particular significance in the city on the north west coast of Spain because it was where the royal family regularly spent their summers. The club is also known as 'La Real'.

Espanyol received the honour in 1912, becoming Real Club Deportivo Espanyol and Real Sporting also traces its title to 1912, after Alfonso XIII accepted the honorary presidency of the Gijon club.

The practice continued through the early 20th century as football rapidly expanded across Spain.

As clubs became established in cities and regions around the country, royal patronage gave some extra prestige. Receiving the 'Real' title could strengthen their social standing while establishing a connection with the country's monarchy.

And then came perhaps the most famous example of all.

Real Madrid was founded in 1902 as Madrid Football Club.

But in 1920, Alfonso XIII granted the club the right to use the title 'Real', with a letter from the monarch's household formally giving the club permission to place the designation before its name. The royal crown was subsequently incorporated into its crest.

There is no sporting qualification needed to become 'Real'. A club does not become 'Real' by winning La Liga, lifting the Copa del Rey, reaching Europe or being promoted to the top flight.

Historically, clubs sought royal patronage and the monarch could grant the designation. Modern examples show that some form of formal request and supporting case can still be made.

That process was demonstrated by Club Deportivo Gara in the small town of Garachico in Tenerife. They play in a league seven tiers below La Liga.

During its centenary celebrations in 2012, the club sought royal recognition. In June that year, the royal house granted the title, allowing the club to become Real Club Deportivo Gara.

Todo ello en una plantilla de 27 futbolistas, por lo que más de la mitad de los jugadores que entrenan con regularidad a las órdenes de Claudio Giráldez habrán pasado, al menos, por el filial céltico.

articles.title: Paul Lambert backs former mentor to turn things around at Celtic
articles.summary: Former Celtic captain Paul Lambert has backed his former mentor Martin O’Neill to turn things around at the hoops in the midst of the recent downturn in fort...
articles.body:
Former Celtic captain Paul Lambert has backed his former mentor Martin O'Neill to turn things around at the hoops in the midst of the recent downturn in fortunes at the club…

IMAGO/Sven Simon. Paul Lambert (vorn) und Stefan Reuter (beide BVB) laufen mit dem Pokal eine Ehrenrunde nach dem Champions League Sieg 1996/1997

Champions League winner Paul Lambert has come out in defence of Martin O'Neill, saying that the veteran Irishman will be hurt by recent criticism in wake of three consecutive losses, which included two against Celtic's most bitter rivals, but never believed for one minute that his job was on the line.

"I think he would have been hurt by the level of criticism," Lambert told BBC Scotland . "You can lose three games in a week, but I think it's just the manner, the way it happened.

"I never thought he would leave. I didn't think the club would sack him but he knows he's not immune from criticism. I think the decision for him, if he wanted to walk away, would be with himself. But it's good that he's staying on because you know what you're getting.

Martin O'Neill speaking to Celtic Player. Screenshot via social media

"I'm pretty sure he won't take what's happened in the last few weeks lying down. Knowing the manager, he's not one to go lightly. He'll try and do everything he can to rectify it. And hopefully the team bounce back when they play Motherwell at the weekend," the former Celtic captain said.

Paul Lambert insisted that the Celtic players must offer more to get their season back on track, as the mini-slump was NOT just down to the manager. The players on the pitch have to shoulder their own share of the blame and also the responsibility of putting things right.

Mika Baur of Celtic celebrates scoring his team's first goal with Camilo Duran during the UEFA Europa League 2026/27 League Phase MD1 match between Celtic FC and Ferencvarosi TC at Celtic Park on September 17, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

"They have to step up," Lambert added. "In the two Rangers games and the European game, they looked a little bit flat and jaded. But I think the rest might have done them good. Players will have looked at themselves and asked, 'am I doing enough?' I think that's what Celtic need.

"They need the characters to come through and actually start to put markers on teams again. You can lose a game and people are coming for you. But they're still at the top of the table, which is good from Celtic's perspective."

Camilo Duran of Celtic celebrates with teammates after scoring his team's second goal during the UEFA Champions League play-offs first leg match between Celtic and LASK at Celtic Park on August 19, 2026. (Photo by Ian MacNicol/Getty Images)

Of course by the time Celtic kick-off against Motherwell at noon on Sunday, the Rangers could top the table by a point for they can beat Neil McCann's Kilmarnock side at Ibrox. It's a match most folk will expect Derek McInnes' side to win so Celtic will need to respond appropriately at Fir Park .

articles.body: Zinedine Zidane es un apasionado del pádel. El seleccionador francés y leyenda del fútbol mundial. En un vídeo promocional en el que Alejandro Galán, número 3 del ránking mundial de pádel, le da la bienvenida, Zidane ha presentado la nueva Adidas Metalbone ZZ Carbon que ya está disponible para los amantes del pádel... y del fútbol. Posteriormente, en una sala con el logo de Adidas, el madrileño coloca la pala ZZ en el centro... y 'Zizou' le acaba regalando sus botas: "Se merecen un buen sitio". El galo sigue teniendo planes para el pádel, y tras haberse expandido los últimos años en Istres (seis pistas al aire libre) y en Turín (centrado en el fútbol sala, con cuatro pistas y varios campus de formación), Zidane trabaja desde hace un año para desembarcar en Madrid, con el Distrito de Hortaleza como sede preferida. articles.title: Everton owners consider selling club two years after takeover
articles.summary: Everton owners the Friedkin Group are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.
articles.body:
Everton owners The Friedkin Group (TFG) are exploring the sale of the club less than two years after taking control.

The American group completed a takeover of the club in 2024 in a deal believed to be worth in excess of £400m.

In a statement, TFG said after prioritising stability, investment and the opening of Everton's new stadium last year, the time is right "to consider the next chapter".

"The Friedkin Group is exploring new investment options for Everton Football Club, including the potential sale of a controlling interest," TFG said.

"When TFG became custodians of Everton, the club faced significant financial uncertainty and challenges both on and off the pitch. The immediate priority was to provide the stability, investment and support needed to secure the club's future, including helping to bring the long-promised stadium to completion for its deserving supporters.

"With that foundation now safely in place, the time is right to consider the next chapter for Everton."

TFG, led by chairman Dan Friedkin, outlined a vision for a "sustainable and successful" future for the club when they took over, but its leadership came under scrutiny during the summer transfer window.

In September, David Moyes said he had never met or spoken to Friedkin, who is based in Houston, since returning as manager in January 2025.

Friedkin leaves the day-to-day running of the club to his son-in-law Rishi Majithia, who works in tandem with chief executive Angus Kinnear.

Fans reacted angrily when news broke that Everton had accepted a £40m bid from Nottingham Forest for one of their prized assets, England Under-19 midfielder Harrison Armstrong.

Everton eventually pulled out of the deal, but supporters remained frustrated by the selling of Beto to Fiorentina shortly after.

The move left the Toffees with just one recognisable striker in 23-year-old Frenchman Thierno Barry.

TFG added that they will only "entertain interest from parties who we strongly believe will be the right stewards to take the club forward".

"Throughout this process, TFG's focus will remain unchanged. We will support the club in all ways necessary to achieve success on the pitch and will continue efforts to make a positive difference in the communities the club serves," the statement continued.

The decision of Everton's owners TFG to explore selling the club comes as no great surprise after the turbulent events of recent times.

A fracture opened up between TFG and Everton's fanbase over the controversial attempt to sell highly-rated teenager Armstrong late in the transfer window, before a botched deadline day left manager Moyes with only 18 senior outfield players.

The failed sale of Armstrong, as well as the departure of Iliman Ndiaye to Manchester City for £65m, was bolted on to a cautious approach to the markets that suggested limited ambition on the part of TFG.

It was in sharp contrast to the more hands-on approach at AS Roma, the other club owned by TFG, who bring in the additional riches of playing in the Champions League.

Moyes revealing he had never spoken to Friedkin, who has not attended an Everton game since the Scot was reappointed as manager 21 months ago, strengthened the belief among supporters that TFG were effectively absentee owners.

TFG secured a deal for 99.5% of the club, succeeding former owner Farhad Moshiri in 2024 after Everton had fallen into financial crisis.

Since then, TFG have put the club on a stable financial footing and Everton have moved into a new stadium - although this was effectively done before their takeover - and have made the club an attractive proposition to potential buyers.

This will be TFG's main achievement in what will, when Everton is sold, be regarded as an unspectacular tenure.

Speaking on 5 Live Breakfast, former Everton goalkeeper Rachel Brown-Finnis described TFG's plans to sell the club as a "shock".

"It's come as a bit of a shock. They have stabilised the club. There was so much financial uncertainty when they arrived, it's felt like a turbulent time," said Brown-Finnis.

"We [Everton] have a stadium to be crazily proud of, it's going to generate revenue from a commercial point of view.

"If the Friedkin Group sells up tomorrow, they have left the club in a much better place. I just hope that they do their due diligence.

"I hope the new owners want to drive the club forward. Everton fans have spent too much time in a financially turbulent era."

articles.title: Enzo Maresca breaks silence on Man City charges and previews Liverpool clash
articles.summary: Enzo Maresca says Manchester City focus remains on Liverpool despite Premier League charges falloutManchester City head coach Enzo Maresca has delivered the...
articles.body:
Enzo Maresca says Manchester City focus remains on Liverpool despite Premier League charges fallout

Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca has delivered the line you would expect from any dressing room trying to survive a storm, keep your head down, train properly and win the next match. The context matters here. City are back in Premier League action against Liverpool at Anfield, with the club still dealing with the fallout after being found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them.

The allegations were serious, the findings were worse, and the timing has left City trying to separate football from everything around it. The Premier League report stated the club had used "sham" contracts to disguise secret funding of more than £830m. That is the backdrop. Maresca's job right now is simpler to describe, far harder to carry out. He has to make sure his players do not drift.

According to Maresca, they have not. "The feeling is fantastic, to be honest," he said ahead of the trip to Anfield. It is a strong message and one clearly designed for both inside and outside the club. He added: "The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league. The players are just focused on that."

Manchester City keep eyes on Premier League race

That is the standard football response, control what you can control, park the noise, get on with it. It also happens to be the only viable one. The squad had several international players returning to training only on Thursday, nine days after the verdict was published, so Maresca had a narrow window to address the issue directly. Internally, the message was straightforward, do not let the crisis damage standards or concentration.

Maresca was equally clear on where he believes the players stand emotionally. "They know what we can control is the football side, they are not worried at all about different things. They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield."

That sounds good. It always does. Whether it holds through 90 minutes at Anfield is another matter. Liverpool away is difficult in clean circumstances. Liverpool away with the club under the harshest scrutiny in English football is something else. Maresca, though, is sticking to the line that the mood remains stable. He said he feels "calm" and that the squad trusts the club "completely".

City have launched an appeal and continue to maintain their innocence publicly. That position has not changed, nor has the message passed privately around the playing group and those connected to it.

Erling Haaland backs City unity before Anfield test

Erling Haaland echoed his manager's position and did so in the language of solidarity rather than legal argument. "I care a lot about this place. I spent my first four years here, it's a special place for us. I care a lot about City and the fans. I am a fan myself. I feel with them."

Again, this is not about evidence, appeals or process. It is about keeping the dressing room and fanbase aligned while the case moves on. Haaland pushed that point further, saying: "The fans will have a good time on Sunday, we have to stick together. We have to stay with each other and stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to smile. Stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and enjoy the situation.

"We have to stick together and spread the love to each other. Enjoy the ride and smile."

There is no tactical revelation in that, but there does not need to be. The striker is reinforcing the same internal brief as the manager. Close ranks. Ignore the outside. Keep winning if possible. For a club trying to preserve normality while facing abnormal circumstances, that is the obvious play.

articles.title: Mourinho reignites Barcelona rivalry with fresh Negreira comments: ‘The problem lies in bad luck’
articles.summary: Jose Mourinho has always been a master at handling media narratives and pushing them in directions that would be beneficial for his team.The Real Madrid mana...
articles.body:
Jose Mourinho has always been a master at handling media narratives and pushing them in directions that would be beneficial for his team.

The Real Madrid manager has now reignited the refereeing debate surrounding Barcelona and Los Blancos .

As quoted by AS , Mourinho was asked about his relationship with referees and responded by referencing the Negreira case.

"I don't think I'm the problem," Mourinho said when questioned about his relationship with referees.

"I think the problem lies in bad luck and arriving at certain clubs at certain times."

"I arrived at Real Madrid during the peak Negreira years."

The Portuguese manager's remarks refer to the period when Barcelona made payments to companies linked to Jose Maria Enriquez Negreira, the former vice-president of Spain's refereeing committee.

Jose Mourinho has always been a master of the media game. (Photo by Denis Doyle/Getty Images)

Those payments have been central to an ongoing legal controversy, although the existence of payments does not, by itself, establish that Barcelona received favourable refereeing decisions.

Mourinho's latest comments revive a familiar argument from his first spell at Madrid, when refereeing disputes regularly dominated discussions surrounding matches against Barcelona.

Barcelona once again drawn into the debate

For Barcelona supporters, Mourinho's remarks are unlikely to come as a surprise.

His first spell at the Bernabeu was marked by an intense rivalry with Pep Guardiola's Barcelona, with controversies involving referees frequently overshadowing the football itself.

He has now arrived in Spain during a time when the Catalan club are enjoying another period of dominance.

Barcelona's sporting achievements during that period cannot simply be dismissed by an allegation, but Madrid are doing their best to push the narrative .

The timing of Mourinho's remarks is particularly interesting with another Clasico approaching later this month.

El Clasico later this month will be exciting. (Photo by Jose Manuel Alvarez Rey/Getty Images)

Barcelona currently hold a six-point advantage over Madrid, and Hansi Flick's side have an opportunity to strengthen their position through their performances.

They do not need to attach too much importance to Mourinho's media antics, nor should they let them affect them negatively.

Flick's side are playing the kind of football that other teams in Spain look to as a reference.

Getting dragged into refereeing debates is unlikely to be healthy for Flick, and it remains to be seen how things play out on this front.

articles.title: Pablo Villa lanza un aviso a Mbappé: “Hasta ahora, el Bernabéu ha sido más condescendiente que exigente”
articles.standfirst: El presentador de La Tribu analiza el regreso del francés al Santiago Bernabéu tras un parón de selecciones marcado por las críticas a su comportamiento fuera del campo
articles.summary: El presentador de La Tribu analiza el regreso del francés al Santiago Bernabéu tras un parón de selecciones marcado por las críticas a su comportamiento fuera del campo
articles.body: Kylian Mbappé regresa al Santiago Bernabéu después de 27 días sin jugar ante su afición. El delantero francés vuelve al estadio madridista tras un parón de selecciones que ha estado rodeado de polémica por su recuperación en París y algunas imágenes de su vida personal. Una situación que ha analizado Pablo Villa en La Tribu, donde ha reflexionado sobre la paciencia que ha tenido hasta ahora el madridismo con su gran estrella. El periodista ha recordado que Mbappé ya ha recibido algún reproche desde la grada por su escasa implicación defensiva, pese a sus extraordinarios registros goleadores. “Los números de Kylian son casi hasta mareantes: 94 goles en 111 partidos, pero vestir la camiseta del Madrid conlleva otras muchas responsabilidades”, ha señalado Villa, recordando también las palabras de José Mourinho: “Jugador del Madrid hay que serlo durante las 24 horas del día”. La recuperación del francés lejos de Valdebebas y sus actividades durante los últimos días han generado numerosas críticas. Para el periodista, Mbappé no ha gestionado de la mejor manera este periodo alejado de la competición: “No ha sido el parón más atinado de Kiki”. Pablo Villa ha repasado los motivos del malestar generado: “Algunos le han criticado por recuperarse en Paris y no en Valdebebas, otros no han entendido la flexibilidad del club con su vuelta y otros muchos han ido más allá centrando sus críticas en su vida personal con sus imágenes nocturnas en la capital francesa o montando en bicicleta”. Pablo Villa también ha querido poner en valor el comportamiento de la afición madridista con el delantero. A pesar de las críticas puntuales, considera que el público del Santiago Bernabéu ha sido más comprensivo que exigente con Mbappé desde su llegada. “La realidad es que el público del Bernabéu puede tener muchos defectos, pero lo que es, sin duda, es justo. Sabe cuándo apretar y cuando ser condescendiente y hasta ahora, ha sido más lo segundo que lo primero con Mbappé”, ha explicado. Una reflexión que ha acompañado de un mensaje sobre las responsabilidades que implica vestir la camiseta blanca: “Porque el Bernabéu no pide santos: exige futbolistas capaces de entender que su escudo pesa incluso cuando los focos se apagan”. Por último, Villa ha dejado una advertencia al francés de cara a su regreso al estadio madridista. “Kylian conoce el camino hacia la portería; ahora le toca recorrer el que conduce al corazón de la grada. Y allí, entre la gloria y la exigencia, no bastará con marcar. También tendrá que convencer”, ha concluido.

articles.title: EFL preview: Savage salvation and a happy homecoming?
articles.summary: Here are the five things across the EFL that you should be keeping your eyes on this weekend.
articles.body:
It takes two weeks inside a chrysalis for a butterfly to emerge, eye-catching in flight, but could the same metamorphosis happen for a football team?

Not all of the English Football League have enjoyed a fortnight off during the international break; teams in League One and League Two have continued their campaigns while a number of players have been off representing their countries.

However, October still offers a fresh start. Close enough to the start of the season for new managers to make an impact in the league, far enough that sides should be finding their footing.

Here are some of the standout fixtures and narratives across the EFL that you should be keeping your eyes on this weekend.

West Bromwich Albion defender Conor Townsend labelled their 1-0 loss to local rivals Wolverhampton Wanderers their "worst performance of the season" but a chance to show they can turn up in a big match has rolled around quickly.

The Baggies return to action with yet more bragging rights on offer, this time welcoming Birmingham City to The Hawthorns on Saturday lunchtime (12:30 BST).

Like Wolves before them, Blues could leapfrog their hosts on the table should they take victory and Albion will be keen to stop allowing their West Midlands foes from using them as a stepping stone closer to the top.

Last season though, the two shared the points in both Championship fixtures with just one goal each - and it was not the only derby to be so tight.

The South Coast meetings between Southampton and Portsmouth last season carried high expectation but both games fell a little flat. In fact, the teams have drawn four of their past five meetings.

Saints may feel a little buoyed this time around though when they meet at St Mary's on Sunday (12:00 BST).

Spygate is finally behind them after boss Tonda Eckert was given a six-week suspended ban for his role in the controversy by the FA.

Portsmouth are on a three match unbeaten run and will be hoping that the media spectacle of Eckert's punishment can prove a suitable distraction for their opponents from the true prize - local pride.

Steven Schumacher left a promoted and thriving Plymouth Argyle to head north to the Bet365 Stadium in December 2023, only to be sacked in September after 32 games.

But, despite the knockback, Schumacher is back in the Championship after leading Bolton to promotion and the Trotters have shown they have plenty of fight in them.

Three of their four losses have been by the margin of a single goal and they have won their past two games to be just three points short of the play-off positions.

His former employers will represent a tough challenge on Saturday (15:00 BST) though with Stoke on a five match undefeated run (W4 D1) and looking to keep consolidating their goal of being a promotion contender.

"At Stoke there has been lots of change, they've moved managers on, they've tried these winning formulas," former Nottingham Forest and Ipswich Town defender Luke Chambers told the 72+ podcast .

"But with Mark Robins, he's a fabulous manager. Stoke City have impressed me, especially within the past few weeks."

Alexander the Great to Preston's rescue?

Graham Alexander is much loved at Deepdale from his playing days, where he made 410 appearances and became club captain.

Fourteen years after his retirement, he is back at the club he claims is "special" to him and with a mammoth challenge on his hands.

The Lilywhites are kept off the bottom spot on the Championship table by just one goal and have managed a solitary win so far this season.

Next they face Millwall on Saturday (15:00 BST), a team that have been beleaguered with injuries but still just two points off the play-off positions.

Conversely, Bradford City will be aiming to show their recent successes have come from more than just possessing Alexander in charge.

Alexander led the Bantams to promotion in 2025 plus a play-off semi-final last season before losing to eventual winners Bolton.

The former Scotland international has left them in pretty good stead too, second on the table level on points with League One leaders Plymouth Argyle.

The man in charge of making sure they continue where they left off is Michael Duff, the former Wycombe Wanderers boss with some big boots to fill.

Duff isn't concerned about the eyes on him though as he prepares for his first game at the helm against Leyton Orient on Saturday (15:00 BST).

"I'm under no illusions, they [the owners] will let you know [if you're doing a bad job]," Duff told the 72+ podcast.

"I like the fact they will because there is an expectancy. It's a big football club. I'd rather have that pressure than playing in front of 200 people that don't care if you win or not."

Robbie Savage has undertaken a huge task in leading Peterborough United away from the bottom side of the table - but it's already got off to a good start.

Posh scored four times in less than 10 minutes for Savage's first game in charge, a 4-1 victory over Ipswich Town in the EFL Trophy.

It brings back times of yore for the club, renowned for their attacking prowess but finding themselves lacking this season as the lowest scorers in League One with just four goals in eight games.

Savage's first chance to make an impression in the third division - and the EFL in general for that matter - is against former club Leicester City, where he made 204 appearances as a player across a five-year stint.

"He is box office, isn't he?" former Middlesbrough defender Tommy Smith told the 72+ podcast. "But he's got a tough start. Three of his next four are away from home. He's got Leicester on Saturday, he's then got Huddersfield and also Bromley."

The two sides meet on Saturday (15:00 BST) and while Russell Martin is still struggling to win over hearts at mind at the King Power Stadium, the Foxes league form has shown some signs of life with a win over Stockport and a draw at Barnsley leading into this fixture.

Things are going mighty well for Salford City and Cheltenham Town as of late.

After three successive losses to open their campaign in August, the Red Devils turnaround to rise to the top spot has earned boss Peter Cklamovski the manager of the month award for September.

Meanwhile, Cheltenham have only lost two games and midfielder Charlie McCann has shown so much influence in the middle of the park that he was named player of the month.

But awards mean nothing if they can't keep the results flowing.

The two meet on the Robins' home turf on Saturday (15:00 BST) and if they win and things go in their favour elsewhere, they could be snatching away Salford's place at the apex.

Even more in their favour, the hosts heavily lead the head-to-head with just two losses in their nine previous meetings (W5 D2).
